newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Cullen calls for RBNZ to enter forex market.
newsitem.headline: Cullen calls for RBNZ to enter forex market.

text.p: Opposition Labour finance spokesman Michael Cullen on Friday called for the Reserve Bank to directly intervene in the foreign exchange market to lower the level of the New Zealand dollar by about 10 percent.
"I think the government and the bank have got to get back to dealing directly in the exchange rate," Cullen told Reuters in an interview.

"The reason is very simple and I have yet to hear any convincing argument against. All I get told is: 'Look what a bath we took when we tried to hold the dollar up and the market wanted to talk it down'.

"No one has explained how the government loses money if it is trying to reduce the value of the dollar and the market insists on it staying up. I think they should think through the mechanics of how that would operate," Cullen said.

"The purpose ... is to get to the real heart of the problem which is to remove the absolute certainty that the dollar is on a steady upwards path. It is not to actually deal so hugely that one temporarily depresses the value."
Cullen said he could not make a useful estimate of the number of dollars the bank would need to sell to achieve his objective.

"What I am sure of is that we have to get some risk back into the foreign exchange market and that would have a significant impact on the Samurai bond issues and all that sort of stuff. Because that is what I think is holding the dollar up
higher than it needs to be."

He said a Bankers Trust Research report commissioned by the Manufacturers Federation and released on Friday showed the entire government spending on health and education would need to be cut to get the dollar down to where it ought to be.
"I reckon we are looking at something close to 10 percent overvalued now (on the Trade-Weighted Index)," Cullen said.
He said the risk was not the same as when former Finance Minister Sir Robert Muldoon tried to defend the dollar in 1984 or when Britain tried to hold up the pound three years ago.
"If you try to hold up an overvalued currency you are always going to take a bath sooner or later. What is the huge risk people think is built in here?"
He rejected the argument New Zealand was too small in relation to the finance flows in its currency to be able to have a lasting impact.
"One of the reasons the finance flows are so large is that people are assuming the dollar keeps going up. Ilfilling prophecy."
He said using interest rates alone would not work. They would have to fall about three percent to lower the currency by 10 percent, and that "would clearly have significant inflationary impact".

He said if the dollar was driven down, interest rates would not go up, but stay roughly where they are now because the RBNZ was happy with their current level. "The mix problem arises only because we are operating only on interest rates."
The RBNZ has said it cannot influence the mix of interest rates and the dollar.

"The point I keep trying to make to people is that central banks or governments ... intervening directly in the exchange rate is not actually unusual in the world. We are unusual in always foreswearing it," Cullen said.
He said threatening to intervene would be a good start.
"Jaw would have significant impact and the fact the government and the bank says:'No jaw' ... the outcome is fairly predictable." -- Wellington newsroom 64 4 473 4746
